Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. Open says the brand is transparent about pricing, providers, and process. Care names the category. The pair reads as a modern alternative to the opaque clinical industry, without trying to be a tech startup.
Modern.industrySummary: Healthcare brand has been clinical, sterile, and slightly intimidating. The modern customer wants clarity: a clean app, clear prices, a doctor they can actually message. New entrants are competing on design and transparency more than on outcomes alone.
Modern.competitorLandscape: One Medical (onemedical.com) holds the modern primary care position. Forward (goforward.com), before its issues, set the tech-led pitch. Parsley Health (parsleyhealth.com) does the wellness-medicine middle. Tia (asktia.com) handles women's health well. We sit closest to One Medical in posture, with a sharper brand surface.
Modern.positioningStatement: Primary care that shows you what it costs before the visit.
Modern.positioningRationale: Most healthcare brands hide the price until after the appointment. Our brand promise is the opposite. Every visit, every test, every prescription is priced clearly on the app before the patient confirms.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 50. Has insurance but doesn't trust it to be transparent. Already pays for at least one premium consumer health app. Wants the doctor visit to feel like booking a flight, not like applying for a mortgage.

dos: Show the price next to the service
Speak to the patient as an adult
Confirm next steps in writing
donts: Photograph models pretending to be patients

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is an open square, three sides of a rectangle suggesting an open door. The mark and the wordmark work together on the front of the clinic, in the app, and on the prescription label.

colorPalette.name: Care Teal
colorPalette.meaning: Health accent. Used like a small green check.

typography.primary: Inter for product UI and headlines
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed patient information
typography.rationale: Inter is the trusted default for clean modern healthcare apps. The serif handles printed patient brochures and the few formal forms.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No surprise billing. No referral lock-in. No upsells in the app. No celebrity-endorsed wellness add-ons. No 'concierge tier' with hidden access.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: An app that books, charges, and confirms in three taps. A clinic that looks like a small library, not a hospital. A printed visit summary at the door. A WhatsApp number for the team that responds within four hours.

Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words that name the only thing patients actually want from primary care — to be seen today. We made the differentiator the name. Reads as both honest and slightly miraculous given what most clinics offer.
Modern.manifesto: Primary care has stopped offering primary care. The average new-patient wait in most cities is now measured in months. We made Same Day because the entire job of primary care is to be available when something small goes wrong. The clinic is built around availability, not appointments.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern primary care has fragmented into urgent care chains and direct-primary-care membership models. The shared customer problem is access. There is a real opening for a brand that competes on time-to-appointment first and everything else second.
Modern.competitorLandscape: One Medical (onemedical.com) holds the membership-primary slot. Forward (goforward.com) sits in the tech-forward middle. Carbon Health (carbonhealth.com) is the urgent-modern peer. We sit further out — same-day-only by policy.
Modern.positioningStatement: Same Day is a primary care clinic that holds half its appointments for today.
Modern.positioningRationale: Half of every day's appointment slots are released that morning. Members and patients book by phone or app for that day. No scheduling six weeks out.

targetAudience.primary: Working adults 25–55 in cities, mostly without a regular doctor.
behaviors: Avoid making appointments because they cannot find a slot.
Use urgent care for primary issues.
Have insurance but rarely use it.
Want to be seen the day the issue starts.
motivations: Want a clinic that opens today.
Want a real doctor, not a video call.
Want to skip the six-week wait.

dos: Lead with today's availability.
Use plain language about the visit.
Reply to inquiries in minutes.
Publish the next-available slot on the home page.
donts: No long onboarding for new patients.
No 'we'll get back to you in 2–3 business days'.

messagingPillars.name: Half held for today
messagingPillars.description: Half of every day's slots are released the morning of. The home page shows how many are left.

messagingPillars.name: Real doctor, real room
messagingPillars.description: Every visit is in-person with a doctor or nurse practitioner. We use telehealth only when the patient asks.

messagingPillars.name: One price, posted
messagingPillars.description: Each visit type has a posted price. Insurance is welcome but optional. Members pay one monthly fee for unlimited visits.

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — SAME DAY set in a calm modern grotesque, all caps, with a small dot indicating availability. Reads as a clinic sign, not a medical brand.

colorPalette.name: Signal
colorPalette.meaning: Accent — a calm clinical green for availability.

typography.primary: A calm modern grotesque for the wordmark and signage.
typography.secondary: A neutral sans for working type and patient materials.
typography.rationale: Two weights, plain register. The clinic does not over-design.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Aldcroft sounds like an English Harley Street practice that has been around for generations. Medical closes it as a clinical service. The whole name reads as a private practice already known to a small set of families.
Luxury.story: Aldcroft began with a single physician who had spent decades inside larger institutional practices and wanted to take fewer patients, more carefully. The practice accepts a limited number of patients each year. Some have been with the practice since it opened.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end medicine has been moving toward concierge-tier products bolted onto larger systems. There's a parallel market for small private practices in the old style. One doctor, a few hundred patients, decades-long relationships. The customer is paying for the practice, the physician, and the next appointment.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Marlowe (themarlowe.com), if it operated in the U.S., would be a peer. Sollis Health (sollishealth.com) holds the concierge tier. K Health (khealth.com) is a digital-first peer. We are closer in spirit to a Harley Street practice than to any of these.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A private medical practice with a limited number of patients and one physician.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often inherited. Values the relationship with the physician. Travels for consultations. Will pay annually for the access, even when nothing is wrong.

dos: Address the patient by surname
Speak in the language of medicine, not wellness
Send paper letters between visits

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn caduceus reduced to two crossed lines, used as a hallmark on letterhead, the brass plaque outside the practice, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

colorPalette.name: Practice Green
colorPalette.meaning: Old leather, library walls, the waiting room.

colorPalette.name: Heritage Brass
colorPalette.meaning: Aged metal. The plaque and the hardware.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and printed material
typography.secondary: Söhne for the secure patient portal
typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles the secure portal and the few digital surfaces.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No public marketing. No social media presence. No press. No celebrity patients on the website. No client logos.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Single proper name with the definite article — the naming convention for a single significant practice. Ashford is a quiet English surname-and-place register that reads as established and slightly Old World. The 'The' signals singular practice, not chain.
Luxury.story: The Ashford Clinic is a private primary care and concierge medicine practice at one location. The roster is capped. The physicians have been at the clinic for over a decade. The practice has no signage on the street.
Luxury.industrySummary: Concierge medicine has grown into a recognizable category but is mostly built around platform models. There is a quieter market for the single-physician-group practice — capped roster, no signage, multi-decade tenure.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: MDVIP (mdvip.com) is the concierge-platform reference. Sollis Health (sollishealth.com) holds the premium concierge slot. Castle Connolly (castleconnolly.com) is the credentialing peer. We sit further out — single building, capped roster, no platform.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The Ashford Clinic is a single-location concierge primary care practice with a capped roster and long-tenure physicians.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not expand. The roster is capped. New patients are accepted by referral. The relationship is the practice.

targetAudience.primary: Adults 40–70 with a long-term relationship with their physician, often family-spanning.
behaviors: Have a single primary physician they have seen for years.
Bring their children to the same practice.
Make decisions about their care in person.
Travel internationally with their medical records.
motivations: Want a practice that knows them across decades.
Want their family in the same practice.

dos: Refer to patients by surname.
Sign correspondence by hand.
Mention the physician by name.
Send printed annual health reviews.

messagingPillars.name: Capped roster
messagingPillars.description: The practice has a fixed cap. New patients are accepted by referral when others move on. The waiting list is real.

messagingPillars.name: Long-tenure physicians
messagingPillars.description: Our senior physicians have been at the clinic for over a decade. Patients see the same doctor across years.

messagingPillars.name: One building, no signage
messagingPillars.description: We do not advertise. The address is on the website for patients only. Outside, the building looks like any other.

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — The Ashford Clinic set in a classical book serif, with a small crest of a single laurel branch. The mark appears in brass on the front door and ink on the letterhead.

typography.primary: A traditional book serif for the wordmark and letterhead.
typography.secondary: An old-style serif for body, generously set.
typography.rationale: Letterpress register throughout. The clinic's communications are mostly printed.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Two words. Check Up is the most basic thing the patient is here for. The brand puts the reason for the visit in the brand position. No clinical jargon. No metaphor. Plain.
Minimal.industrySummary: Healthcare brands lead with promises, partnerships, and proprietary protocols. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the visit itself. One reason to come in. One appointment. Done.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most consumer healthcare brands compete on apps, programs, and continuity. We compete on simplicity. The closest peers in spirit are some Japanese clinics and the early Walgreens Healthcare Clinic model.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A clinic for the check up and nothing else.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who don't have a primary care doctor and don't want one. They want to come in, get checked, and leave. They will pay fairly for that and resent paying for anything else.

dos: Show the appointment slot
Show the price
Send the result by SMS

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. CHECK UP in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, two words on a single line. No icon. The signage uses the wordmark and the appointment number. That's the whole system.

typography.rationale: One face. The reception, the SMS confirmation, and the printed receipt all use the same wordmark.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No subscription. No app. No newsletter. No wellness programs. No referrals to specialists we partner with.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: One word. The action the patient takes. We named the clinic after the visit and stopped. Reads as plain, slightly clinical in a good way — the building exists for the visit.
Minimal.manifesto: Healthcare brand vocabulary has run away from the room. Wellness, vitality, journey, partnership, optimization. We made Visit because the only thing a clinic is for is the visit. Come in. We see you. You leave.
Minimal.industrySummary: Primary care marketing has drifted into wellness vocabulary. There is room for a clinic that names the actual unit — the visit — and does it plainly.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Forward (goforward.com) holds the modern-minimal middle. Parsley Health (parsleyhealth.com) sits in the wellness-minimal slot. One Medical (onemedical.com) is the broad peer. We sit further out — the clinic surface is shorter than any of theirs.
Minimal.positioningStatement: VISIT is a clinic that books visits, plainly, at posted prices.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the clinic surface. The site is a list of visit types, a list of prices, and a button. The visit is the product.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who use healthcare occasionally and want the path short.
behaviors: See a doctor once or twice a year.
Skip the patient portal.
Want one bill, not three.
Compare price and proximity.
motivations: Want a clean clinic, a quick visit, a single bill.
Want to skip the wellness marketing.
Want a list of visit types and prices.

dos: List the visits. List the prices.
Confirm bookings in one line.
Send aftercare instructions as a short note.
Sign emails with the clinic's name only.

messagingPillars.name: Posted prices
messagingPillars.description: Every visit type has a posted price. The page is a list of visits and prices and a button. Insurance optional.

messagingPillars.name: One visit, one bill
messagingPillars.description: Each visit produces one bill. We do not separate facility and physician fees.

messagingPillars.name: Aftercare as a note
messagingPillars.description: Aftercare instructions are a short, plain note. No portal login. The note arrives by email and on paper.

Minimal.logoDirection: VISIT set in a neutral grotesque, all caps, at small scale on the door, the bill, and nowhere else. No emblem.

colorPalette.name: Mark
colorPalette.usage: The visit-type chip and primary action.

typography.primary: One neutral grotesque, regular and medium.
typography.secondary: Same family for tables and bills.
typography.rationale: One typeface across the door, the bill, and the aftercare note.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Sentinel suggests vigilance, watching, standing guard. Health Group names the category. The whole name reads like a real, established healthcare services firm, the kind already on procurement panels at large companies and health systems.
Corporate.industrySummary: Healthcare services contracted to enterprise customers (employers, health systems, payers) is a serious B2B category. Buyers want operational reliability, regulatory-grade reporting, and a partner who can stand up programs across multiple sites.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Optum (optum.com) is the giant. Cleveland Clinic for Business (clevelandclinic.org) holds the clinical-prestige B2B side. Crossover Health (crossoverhealth.com) sits in the employer-health middle. We sit smaller than Optum, more design-led than Crossover.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Healthcare operations for self-insured employers and health system partners.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Self-insured employers and regional health systems want operational partners who can deliver reliable care programs without the bureaucratic overhead of the giant vendors. We win on responsiveness and reporting depth.

targetAudience.primary: Heads of Benefits, Chief Medical Officers, and Population Health Directors at self-insured employers and regional health systems. They sign multi-year contracts.
motivations: Regulatory-grade reporting on outcomes and spend
One partner across employee health, occupational, and clinical services

dos: Lead with reporting and outcomes
Show cohort metrics in case studies
Speak to the buyer, not the patient

messagingPillars.name: Operations at scale
messagingPillars.description: Care delivered consistently across multiple employer sites and regional health systems.

messagingPillars.name: Reporting that meets the standard
messagingPillars.description: Outcomes, utilization, and ROI reports formatted to the standard the chief medical officer and CFO both need.

messagingPillars.name: One partner across services
messagingPillars.description: Onsite clinics, virtual care, occupational health, and population health under one contract.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is a single shield silhouette with a horizontal divider, suggesting protection and structure. Reads cleanly on uniforms, vans, badges, and procurement decks.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and product UI
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed quarterly reports
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles formal quarterly health reports and clinical documentation.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No D2C app. No retail clinics. No celebrity health endorsements. The firm sells through enterprise procurement, not Instagram health content.

Corporate.tagline: Multi-specialty primary care and ambulatory services.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Coombe is a surname pulled from older medical practice naming — quiet, slightly Anglo-Irish, professional. Medical Partners signals the partner-led organizational structure. The pair reads as a long-standing physician group, not a venture-funded clinic chain.
Corporate.manifesto: Coombe Medical Partners is a physician-owned multi-specialty group serving primary care, internal medicine, and ambulatory services across multiple sites. The buyer is a health system, an employer benefits team, or a regional payer. The relationship is the multi-year contract. The metric is patient outcomes and operational reliability.
Corporate.industrySummary: Multi-specialty physician groups face consolidation pressure from health systems and private equity. The opening is for a physician-owned group with operational depth, integrated billing, and quality metrics that hold up to payer scrutiny.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Privia Health (priviahealth.com) is the platform reference. Iora Health (iorahealth.com) holds the value-based peer slot. ChenMed (chenmed.com) plays in the senior-care middle. We sit in the regional physician-owned multi-specialty category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Coombe Medical Partners is a physician-owned multi-specialty group operating primary care and ambulatory services across a regional footprint.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on quality metrics, payer contract performance, and physician retention. The group is owned by the physicians, not by a platform.

targetAudience.primary: Health systems, employer benefits teams, regional payers, and physician groups considering joining a larger partnership.
behaviors: Review quality metrics across multi-specialty groups.
Contract on value-based and capitated arrangements.
Care about HEDIS scores and readmission rates.
Renew on multi-year terms.
motivations: Want a physician-owned partner with measured quality.
Want a partner whose physicians stay long-term.

dos: Lead with quality metrics, payer mix, and physician tenure.
Speak the language of health-system administrators and payers.
Publish a quarterly group performance review.
Refer to the physicians by name in correspondence.
donts: No consumer marketing in the group voice.

messagingPillars.name: Physician-owned
messagingPillars.description: The group is owned and governed by the practicing physicians. Decisions are made at the partner level, not by external investors.

messagingPillars.name: Quality on paper
messagingPillars.description: We publish HEDIS, MIPS, and readmission performance annually. Payers receive quarterly performance reports tied to contract terms.

messagingPillars.name: Multi-specialty, one site footprint
messagingPillars.description: Primary care, internal medicine, women's health, behavioral health, and ambulatory services across a coordinated regional footprint.

Corporate.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Coombe set in a traditional book serif, with 'Medical Partners' beneath in tracked small caps and a small caduceus mark. Letterhead register.

typography.primary: A traditional book serif for the wordmark and letterhead.
typography.secondary: A clean enterprise grotesque for documents, forms, and reports.
typography.rationale: Tables and numbers tabular and disciplined.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. House Call is the older word for the doctor coming to the patient's home. It belongs to a different era of medicine and a different relationship. The name reframes modern primary care as a relationship, not a transaction.
Creative.manifesto: Most healthcare brands sound like an insurance company trying to be your friend. They overpromise, underexplain, and outsource the warmth. House Call is the brand for the doctor who knows your name, has been to your kitchen, and won't pretend the system is fine. Warm, sharp, honest about what's broken.
Creative.industrySummary: Healthcare branding has been polished, professional, and a little cold. There's room for one that's warm, personable, sticker-friendly, and still serious about the work.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Parsley Health (parsleyhealth.com) does warm-modern. Tia (asktia.com) holds the design-forward women's health position. Galileo (galileo.io) sits in the digital-first peer group. We sit warmer than all of them, with a clearer point of view.
Creative.positioningStatement: A primary care brand that treats the patient like a person, not a chart.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Has insurance, doesn't trust it. Already pays out of pocket for at least one health service. Wants the doctor to actually know them. Will pay for the relationship.

dos: Talk like the family doctor who would call you back
Be honest about what's broken in the system
Make jokes about the bureaucracy

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display serif with the C of CALL stylized as a small doorbell or knocker. Standalone doorbell icon for app icons, social profiles, and the front door of the clinic. The mark reads warm and a little old-fashioned, which is the point.

colorPalette.name: House Red
colorPalette.meaning: Warm, loud, the front door of a clinic.

colorPalette.name: Anchor Navy
colorPalette.meaning: Clinical trust, used as a counter to the warm tone.

typography.primary: Migra for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and signage
typography.rationale: Migra has warmth and character. Neue Montreal handles the practical patient information. The pair feels designed and human.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not a wellness brand. Not a tech-first telehealth brand. Not afraid of red. Not too cool to call you back.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A clinic that feels like a kitchen. A printed visit summary mailed in a real envelope. Text messages from the doctor, written by the doctor. A monthly newsletter that's actually written by a person on the team.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words that pick a fight with the entire industry. No Waiting is what every waiting room sign should say and never does. We made the contrarian promise the name. Sets the expectation before the patient walks in.
Creative.manifesto: We made No Waiting because waiting rooms are the lie at the heart of healthcare. You arrive at the appointment time. You wait forty minutes. The visit lasts twelve minutes. We started a clinic that flips the math. The waiting room has six chairs and is mostly empty. If we are running late, we say so before you arrive and we credit the visit fee.
Creative.industrySummary: Patient satisfaction surveys consistently identify wait time as the largest source of clinic frustration. No clinic brand has chosen wait time as its primary positioning. There is a real opening for a brand that competes on the waiting-room metric.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Forward (goforward.com) touches operational efficiency. One Medical (onemedical.com) holds the modern-experience slot. Crossover Health (crossoverhealth.com) is the employer-onsite peer. We sit further out — the brand is the clock.
Creative.positioningStatement: No Waiting is a clinic that runs to time and credits the visit fee when it does not.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand makes a public promise about wait time and stakes the visit fee on it. The clinic is operationally built around the promise.

targetAudience.primary: Working adults who have stopped going to the doctor because of how long it takes.
behaviors: Schedule visits around their work calendar.
Resent waiting rooms.
Avoid annual physicals.
Use urgent care because primary care is unreachable.
motivations: Want a clinic that respects their calendar.
Want a visit that starts on time.
Want a clinic willing to bet on its own promise.

dos: State the promise plainly.
Publish wait-time data weekly.
Notify patients in advance if running late.
Use the brand line — 'no waiting' — on every door.
donts: No magazines in the waiting room — there is no waiting room to fill.

messagingPillars.name: The promise
messagingPillars.description: Your visit starts within 5 minutes of your scheduled time. If it does not, we credit the visit fee that day.

messagingPillars.name: Six-chair waiting room
messagingPillars.description: We build the schedule, the staffing, and the rooms around the promise. The waiting room has six chairs and is mostly empty.

messagingPillars.name: Weekly wait-time report
messagingPillars.description: We publish actual median and 95th-percentile wait times by week on the website. Members get the report by email.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — NO WAITING set in a wide modern grotesque with a small clock mark beside it. The clock hands point to the next available slot.

colorPalette.name: Signal
colorPalette.meaning: Accent — used for the clock and the timer.
colorPalette.usage: The wordmark mark, the wait-time chip.

typography.primary: A wide modern grotesque for the wordmark and the clinic signage.
typography.secondary: A neutral sans for working type.
typography.rationale: The wordmark is the promise. The body type is the schedule.
